# VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning

Meng Lu Affiliation: Virginia Tech Affiliation: Cisco    Ligeng Zhu
Affiliation: NVIDIA    Olivia Xiao Affiliation: UChicago    Yuchen
Zhuang Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Zihan Wang Affiliation: Abaka AI   
Kuncheng Wu Affiliation: UC Berkeley    Bangya Liu Affiliation: Abaka AI
   Yu Wang Affiliation: UGA    Charles Fleming Affiliation: Cisco   
Wenqi Shi Affiliation: WashU    Xuan Wang Affiliation: Virginia Tech

###### Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a
standard recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs), but it
typically assumes a static training environment. As the actor improves,
fixed tasks drift out of its learning frontier: many become trivial,
others remain unsolvable; and the learning signal collapses. We argue
that _VLM post-training should evolve the visual environment alongside
the actor_, not just the actor itself. We propose VICO, a
co-evolutionary framework in which an _actor_ and an
_Environment-as-Rewriter_ (EnvRewriter) are trained jointly: the
EnvRewriter edits verifiable image-side structures, such as scene
graphs, chart tables, or protected region masks, and re-renders them to
produce label-valid training samples whose difficulty is calibrated to
the actor’s current ability through a pass-rate-based reward. This loop
continuously realigns task difficulty with actor capability without any
additional human annotation. Across nine multimodal benchmarks spanning
mathematical reasoning and visually grounded understanding, VICO-8B
improves over its base model by up to +5.0% on out-of-domain tasks,
surpasses the strongest self-evolution and text-editing co-evolution
baselines by +4.3% and +8.4% respectively, and stays comparable to
chart-specialized RLVR methods using 16–160$`\times`$ fewer labeled
samples. By shifting from human-labeled supervision to image-editing
co-evolution, VICO offers a scalable path beyond static-corpus RLVR for
visual reasoning.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.10782v1/teaser-L-2.png)

Figure 1: Co-evolution with adaptive visual environments and actors
leads to better training.

Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have recently improved through
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
(RLVR) \[[14](#bib.bib23)\], where models learn from automatically
checkable outcomes rather than dense human
rationales \[[31](#bib.bib2)\]. This recipe has made self-evolution an
attractive paradigm: rather than relying on costly human supervision, a
model can generate tasks, collect rollouts, and improve from its own
experience \[[22](#bib.bib3), [38](#bib.bib4)\]. Yet most self-evolution
pipelines share a structural limitation: the actor keeps changing, but
the visual environment stays fixed. As the actor improves, fixed tasks
drift out of its learning frontier, where many become trivial while
others remain unsolvable. In both regimes, the rollout group provides
little useful contrast
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")):
the empirical pass rate $`\hat{p}`$ moves toward $`1`$ or $`0`$, the
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reward variance, proportional
to $`\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})`$, collapses, and the learning signal weakens
precisely when the actor is ready to learn more \[[15](#bib.bib5)\].
Crucially, $`\hat{p}`$ already tells us exactly how difficult each task
is for the current actor, yet existing methods use it only for
normalization or filtering, discarding a signal that could otherwise
guide the environment itself. This raises the central question of our
work: _can the visual environment adapt to the actor using the same
rollout feedback that trains the actor?_

Answering this question (i.e., adapting the visual environment),
however, requires more than simply generating new images. Useful
training samples must satisfy two constraints simultaneously. First,
they should be _verifiable_: edits should not introduce ambiguous
questions or incorrect labels, otherwise the verifiable reward signal
that underpins RLVR breaks down. Second, they should be
_capability-aligned_: edits should move tasks toward the actor’s current
learning frontier rather than making them arbitrarily harder or easier.
Human annotation \[[26](#bib.bib11), [25](#bib.bib6)\] satisfies both
but does not scale, while offline augmentation with stronger
teachers \[[7](#bib.bib51), [24](#bib.bib50)\] reduces annotation cost
but produces a static distribution that cannot track the actor’s
evolving weaknesses. What is missing is an automatic visual environment
that adapts to the actor while preserving the validity of the label.

We propose VICO, a co-evolution framework that addresses both
requirements through joint training of two VLMs. The _actor_ learns to
answer visual reasoning questions, while the _EnvRewriter_ learns to
perform verifiable structured edits to match the actor’s current
ability. For each rewritten task, we sample a group of actor rollouts
and reuse the resulting pass rate $`\hat{p}`$ as a shared learning
signal: binary rollout rewards update the actor through GRPO, while
$`\hat{p}`$ updates the EnvRewriter through an $`\alpha`$-curriculum
reward that peaks near $`\hat{p}=0.5`$, steering edits into the actor’s
_learnable zone_. We then evaluate VICO across three representative
visual reasoning domains, including compositional reasoning, chart
understanding, and general visual question answering, and against three
categories of baselines: text-only rewriting, static-environment
self-evolution, and offline augmentation with stronger teachers,
including GPT-5 \[[29](#bib.bib52)\] and Nano
Banana \[[12](#bib.bib53)\]. Across eight out-of-distribution
benchmarks, VICO exceeds the strongest self-evolution baseline by +4.3%
on average. Notably, even when stronger image generators are scaled up,
static baselines plateau, indicating that the gains stem from the
iterative actor–environment loop rather than from data generation
quality alone. Our contributions are as follows:

- •
  An actor–environment co-evolution paradigm for VLM reasoning. We
  introduce a framework in which the visual environment evolves
  alongside the actor, using the rollout pass rate $`\hat{p}`$ as a
  shared learning signal. This continually realigns task difficulty with
  actor capability and overcomes the saturation that limits
  fixed-environment self-evolution.
- •
  A verifiable image-editing training framework. We design a pipeline
  that couples structured visual editing with RLVR, converting edited
  images into valid training samples through deterministic rendering and
  programmatic relabeling, with no human annotation.
- •
  Strong empirical performance across diverse benchmarks. Across nine
  multimodal benchmarks, VICO surpasses RLVR baselines by +15.5% on
  average, exceeds the strongest self-evolution baseline by +4.3% on
  out-of-domain tasks, and outperforms the proprietary Gemini-2.5-Pro by
  +2.5%.
- •
  Annotation-efficient training. VICO is competitive with
  chart-specialized RLVR methods using 16$`\times`$–160$`\times`$ fewer
  labeled samples, demonstrating that adaptive environments can
  substitute for large-scale human or teacher-model annotation.

## 2 Related Work

##### Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language Reasoning.

RLVR has become a standard post-training recipe for language and
vision-language models, replacing dense human rationales with rule- or
program-checkable outcomes \[[21](#bib.bib22), [31](#bib.bib2)\]. Recent
multimodal extensions of RLVR target multi-step visual reasoning through
cross-modal symbolic formalization \[[45](#bib.bib15)\], scaled
rule-based reward training \[[27](#bib.bib16)\], and combined SFT-RL
pipelines \[[10](#bib.bib17)\]. Subsequent work refines RLVR through
efficient visual processing \[[44](#bib.bib26)\], weakness-driven
problem generation \[[23](#bib.bib27)\], curiosity-driven
exploration \[[9](#bib.bib28)\], and multi-turn world-model
reasoning \[[36](#bib.bib29)\]. While these methods differ in reward
design, exploration strategy, and training schedule, they share a common
assumption: a fixed pool of visual tasks. _VICO instead treats the
visual environment as a learnable component that co-adapts with the
actor_, aiming to unlock new capabilities rather than refine existing
ones over a static distribution \[[48](#bib.bib30)\].

##### Self-Evolving VLMs.

Self-evolving VLMs reduce reliance on human-curated supervision by
letting models generate, solve, or refine their own training data.
MM-Zero bootstraps multimodal reasoning from zero labeled data by
proposing and solving visual problems \[[22](#bib.bib3)\], VisPlay
self-generates question-answer pairs from raw images for RL
training \[[17](#bib.bib31)\], and Vision-Zero frames self-improvement
as visual self-play with verifiable outcomes \[[38](#bib.bib4)\].
Related efforts apply self-evolution to visual games \[[43](#bib.bib32),
[34](#bib.bib33)\], perception \[[50](#bib.bib34)\], image-quality
assessment \[[40](#bib.bib35)\], self-refinement \[[11](#bib.bib36)\],
and OCR hallucination mitigation \[[18](#bib.bib37)\]. Across these
methods, the actor evolves but the visual environment remains fixed,
leaving the training distribution increasingly misaligned with the
actor’s current ability.

##### Co-Evolving VLMs and Environments.

A more recent line of co-evolution work allows the environment to change
with the model: GenEnv trains an environment policy for
difficulty-aligned planning tasks \[[15](#bib.bib5)\], V-Zero perturbs
the textual side of visual tasks while keeping the image pool
fixed \[[35](#bib.bib18)\], C2-Evo co-evolves multimodal data and model
training through model-driven generation \[[8](#bib.bib38)\], and
Active-Zero retrieves from a large external image pool in an offline
augmentation setting \[[16](#bib.bib49)\]. VICO differs from this line
in two ways: it edits the visual substructure of each image rather than
perturbing text or retrieving from a fixed pool, directly adapting the
modality where reasoning is grounded; and it uses the actor’s own pass
rate as the supervision for environment updates, providing a
difficulty-calibration loop tightly coupled to the actor’s learning
trajectory.

![Refer to caption](2610.10782v1/overview.png)

Figure 2: VICO turns self-evolution into an adaptive actor–environment
loop. The EnvRewriter creates visual tasks, the Actor solves them, and
shared rollouts update both policies: task rewards train the Actor,
while difficulty-aligned rewards train the EnvRewriter.

## 3 Methodology

VICO views visual reasoning training as an _actor-environment curriculum
process_ rather than a single model self-optimization problem. We
maintain two policies: an _actor_ $`\pi_{a}`$ (the vision-language model
being trained) and an _EnvRewriter_ $`\pi_{R}`$ (the environment that
produces training samples). Unlike standard RLVR with a fixed training
source, VICO enables both to co-evolve: $`\pi_{a}`$ learns to solve
visual reasoning tasks whose difficulty is shaped by the current
EnvRewriter, while $`\pi_{R}`$ is rewarded for producing edited images
whose difficulty is aligned with the actor’s current capability —
targeting the “learnable zone” where the learning signal is most
effective.

### 3.1 Data-Evolving Paradigm: From Static RLVR to Adaptive Co-evolution

Standard RLVR minimizes a loss $`\mathcal{L}(\theta)`$ over a static
dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{static}}=\{(x,q,a)\}`$, where $`\theta`$
denotes the parameters of the actor. In contrast, VICO implements a
_Data-Evolving Paradigm_. At each round $`t`$, the training dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ is generated dynamically by the EnvRewriter
$`\pi_{R}`$, based on the actor’s current pass rate. This establishes a
feedback loop
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Co-Evolving VLMs and Environments. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"))
in which the EnvRewriter’s goal is not to beat the actor, but to
identify its “breaking points” and convert them into a training signal.

### 3.2 Seed Visual Data and Verifiable Sample Generation

We start VICO from a small seed visual dataset and let the EnvRewriter
derive additional training examples by editing the structured or
protected representation of each seed sample in subsequent rounds. The
key requirement is that every edited sample remains _label-valid_ while
its difficulty changes. We therefore avoid unconstrained pixel-level
generation. Instead, the answer can either be recomputed
programmatically from the edited structure or preserved by construction
through constrained editing.
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Seed Visual Data and Verifiable Sample Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
summarizes the editing interface for each domain.

|                              |                                                                                                               |                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Domain                       | Editing Interface                                                                                             | Label-Validity Rule                                                                                                                               |
| CLEVR \[[19](#bib.bib24)\]   | Edit the scene graph: attributes, objects, shapes, or relations.                                              | Re-execute the question program on the edited graph; reject rendering or ambiguity failures.                                                      |
| ChartQA \[[26](#bib.bib11)\] | Edit the CSV table under a two-tier rule: Tier 1 has a unique answer cell; Tier 2 has no unique cell mapping. | Tier 1 computes $`a^{\prime}=\mathrm{table}^{\prime}[r,c]`$; Tier 2 preserves $`a^{\prime}=a`$. Reject schema, rendering, or invariance failures. |
| ZwZ \[[39](#bib.bib39)\]     | Edit only the complement of protected target masks, e.g., background or non-target distractors.               | Preserve $`(q^{\prime},a^{\prime})=(q,a)`$; reject edits whose mask overlaps protected targets or fails rendering.                                |

Table 1: VICO keeps edited samples verifiable across domains. Structured
domains use deterministic recomputation, while natural images use
constrained answer preservation; neither needs judging or relabeling.

We experiment with three types of data: $`2{,}000`$ CLEVR with scene
graphs and question programs, $`2{,}000`$ ChartQA with their underlying
CSV tables, and $`1{,}000`$ ZwZ with answer-relevant region annotations.
The actor–environment co-evolution loop is shared across all three
domains; only the verifiable editing interface depends on the structure
available in each dataset. More details are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Data Sources and Verifiable Visual Editing ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
We further analyze seed-sampling stability in
Appendix [H.5](#A8.SS5 "H.5 Stability Across Random Seeds ‣ Appendix H Ablation and Robustness Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning");
three ChartQA runs with different seed samples fluctuate by less than
$`2\%`$.

### 3.3 Rewards and Co-Evolutionary Optimization

##### Actor Reward and Update.

The EnvRewriter generates a training instance
$`(x^{\prime},q^{\prime},a^{\prime})`$ with a verified answer
$`a^{\prime}`$, where $`a^{\prime}`$ is programmatically computed from
the modified structured representation
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Data Sources and Verifiable Visual Editing ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")).
This verifiable answer enables rule-based rewards, avoiding neural
reward models that are prone to reward hacking. The actor’s response
receives a reward $`+1`$ if it both produces the correct answer (exact
match against $`a^{\prime}`$) and follows the required
\<think\>/\<answer\> format; otherwise, it receives $`-1`$
(Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Reward Functions and Difficulty Filtering ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")) \[[52](#bib.bib25)\].
The actor $`\pi_{a}`$ is updated to maximize this reward via
GRPO \[[31](#bib.bib2)\] on edited triples sampled from
$`\mathcal{D}_{a}`$.

##### EnvRewriter Reward and Update.

The core innovation for $`\pi_{R}`$ is a difficulty-calibration reward
that targets a success-rate band around $`\alpha=0.5`$. For each edited
image $`x^{\prime}`$, the actor generates $`K`$ rollouts, and we compute
the empirical pass rate $`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}`$ as the fraction of
correct rollouts. The EnvRewriter reward is a bell-shaped function of
$`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}`$ peaked at $`\alpha`$
(Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Reward Functions and Difficulty Filtering ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")),
which discourages edits that are already mastered
($`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}\to 1`$) or hopeless
($`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}\to 0`$). We additionally apply a difficulty
filter that excludes edits with
$`|\hat{p}_{\text{final}}-\alpha|>k_{\min}`$ from EnvRewriter updates,
where $`k_{\min}\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}]`$ is the maximum allowed deviation
from $`\alpha`$, to prevent overfitting to transient spikes; a
theoretical justification is provided in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Theoretical Analysis of Difficulty-Calibrated VICO ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
The EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}`$ is updated via Reward-Weighted Regression
(RWR) on a weighted SFT set of edit trajectories, with stability ensured
by a KL penalty to the initial EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}^{(0)}`$ and a
maximum KL threshold $`\delta_{\max}`$.
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 VICO: Algorithm Details ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ B.1 VICO: Algorithm Details ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
summarizes the full optimization loop.

## 4 Theoretical Analysis of Difficulty-Calibrated VICO

We provide a simple analysis to clarify two properties of VICO’s
co-evolution mechanism. First, edits with pass rates close to
$`\alpha=0.5`$ provide the strongest learning signal for the actor.
Second, as the actor matures, the optimal target can shift away from
$`0.5`$, which explains the saturation observed in our experiments. Full
derivations are deferred to
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Theoretical Analysis and Saturation ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

##### Intermediate difficulty maximizes the actor’s learning signal.

Consider a stylized bandit setting where the actor receives a binary
reward $`r\in\{0,1\}`$ with success probability $`p`$ on an edited image
$`x^{\prime}`$. Under a REINFORCE-style update \[[41](#bib.bib48)\] with
a variance-minimizing baseline \[[20](#bib.bib43)\], and under a
standard bounded-score assumption for policy-gradient updates, the
squared gradient norm satisfies

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathbb{E}\big[\|g(x^{\prime},r)\|^{2}\big]\;\propto\;p(1-p),
       ```                                                            |     | (4.1) |

up to constants independent of $`p`$. Since $`p(1-p)`$ is concave and
maximized at $`p=1/2`$, the gradient signal is strongest for edits of
intermediate difficulty. Equivalently, maximizing $`p(1-p)`$ is the same
as minimizing $`(p-\tfrac{1}{2})^{2}`$. This supports adopting the
$`\alpha`$-Curriculum reward \[[15](#bib.bib5)\]
$`R_{\text{rewriter}}(\hat{p})=\exp(-\beta(\hat{p}-\alpha)^2)`$ with
$`\alpha=0.5`$ as the difficulty-calibration objective for the
EnvRewriter.

##### A drift-corrected target predicts saturation.

The target $`\alpha=0.5`$ is optimal only when edits are costless. As
the actor improves, its pass rate $`\hat{p}_{\text{orig},t}`$ on the
unedited image rises. Forcing the edited sample back to $`\hat{p}=0.5`$
may then require increasingly aggressive edits. These edits can move the
training distribution away from the natural image
manifold \[[1](#bib.bib42)\]. We model this trade-off by adding a
quadratic drift penalty:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\Delta\text{Acc}_{t}=C_{t}p(1-p)-\lambda\kappa_{t}(p-\hat{p}_{\text{orig},t})^{2},
``` |  | (4.2) |

where $`C_{t}>0`$ denotes the actor’s remaining learning headroom, and
$`\lambda\kappa_{t}\geq 0`$ controls the drift cost. Maximizing this
concave objective gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p^{*}_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\rho_{t}\left(\hat{p}_{\text{orig},t}-\tfrac{1}{2}\right),\quad\rho_{t}=\frac{\lambda\kappa_{t}}{C_{t}+\lambda\kappa_{t}}\in[0,1],
``` |  | (4.3) |

so the optimal target is a convex combination of $`0.5`$ and
$`\hat{p}_{\text{orig},t}`$. When the actor has large headroom
($`\rho_{t}\to 0`$), the optimal target remains near $`0.5`$. As
headroom shrinks or drift cost increases ($`\rho_{t}\to 1`$), the
optimum moves toward the unedited pass rate. Continued editing then
enters a drift-dominated regime, where stronger perturbations bring
smaller gains and may eventually hurt performance. This analysis
predicts diminishing per-round gains, fewer sweet-zone samples, and
eventual saturation, which we verify in
Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Empirical Saturation Evidence ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Analysis and Saturation ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

##### Training Setup.

For the Actor $`\pi_{a}`$, we train via GRPO \[[31](#bib.bib2)\] with
$`n=8`$ on-policy rollouts and a learning rate $`1\!\times\!10^{-6}`$.
The EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}`$ is updated via reward-weighted LoRA SFT with
$`\beta=4.0`$ and $`\alpha=0.5`$ (\[[15](#bib.bib5)\]). We use AdamW for
both policies, run VICO for $`T=5`$ rounds, and use up to
$`8\!\times\!\text{A100-80GB}`$ GPUs with verl \[[32](#bib.bib19)\]. We
train Qwen3-VL-8B \[[2](#bib.bib14)\] on three visual datasets, and
Qwen2.5-VL-7B \[[3](#bib.bib21)\] and InternVL3-8B \[[53](#bib.bib20)\]
on chart understanding to assess backbone generalizability. We validate
VICO on three visual reasoning domains: CLEVR \[[19](#bib.bib24)\] for
compositional reasoning, ChartQA \[[26](#bib.bib11)\] for chart
reasoning, and ZwZ \[[39](#bib.bib39)\] for natural-image VQA. Full
hyperparameters, two-stage training, dataset examples, and multi-seed
analyzes are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

##### Tasks and Datasets.

We evaluate on nine benchmarks under identical zero-shot settings
(temperature $`0.7`$, top-$`p`$ $`1.0`$, max response length $`3{,}824`$
tokens). For mathematical reasoning, we use
MathVista \[[25](#bib.bib6)\], MathVision \[[37](#bib.bib7)\],
MathVerse \[[51](#bib.bib8)\], WeMath \[[30](#bib.bib9)\], and
LogicVista \[[42](#bib.bib10)\]. For chart reasoning, we use
ChartQA \[[26](#bib.bib11)\]. For general vision-centric understanding,
we use MMMU \[[47](#bib.bib12)\], MMVP \[[49](#bib.bib40)\], and
BLINK \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. The Average column in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
is the equally weighted average of the mathematical-reasoning average
and the vision-centric average.

##### Baselines.

We compare VICO against three categories of strong baselines reflecting
different post-training paradigms: (1) RLVR-trained reasoning models
trained with RLVR on human-labeled
data—R1-OneVision-7B \[[45](#bib.bib15)\],
MM-Eureka-Qwen-7B \[[27](#bib.bib16)\],
OpenVLThinker-7B \[[10](#bib.bib17)\]; (2) Self-evolution models that
evolve the model in a fixed environment—MM-Zero-8B \[[22](#bib.bib3)\],
three VisionZero-7B variants (CLEVR, Chart, Real-world), and
VisionZero-InternVL3-8B \[[38](#bib.bib4)\]; (3) Co-evolution baseline
V-Zero \[[35](#bib.bib18)\], which perturbs question-answer pairs
without editing the visual environment. These three categories isolate
the effect of *visual-environment co-evolution* from data-rich RL
post-training and model-side self-evolution. Implementation details are
in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

### 5.2 Main Results

VICO-actor consistently improves over the base model and outperforms
three categories of baselines: RL-trained reasoning models, self- and
co-evolution methods.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
presents the main comparison. For the Chart Understanding variant, we
report the OOD average over the eight benchmarks excluding ChartQA,
which is its in-domain benchmark. For the CLEVR and ZwZ variants, all
nine evaluation benchmarks are treated as out-of-domain. Notably, VICO
attains these improvements using only 2000 seed inputs, which is
$`16\times`$–$`160\times`$ fewer than the chart-specialized RLVR
baselines that depend on large amounts of human or model-generated CoT
annotations
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")).
The strongest variant, VICO-8B (Chart), achieves the best OOD average
accuracy of $`64.9\%`$ (excluding in-domain ChartQA), improving over the
base model by $`+5.0\%`$. Against RL-trained reasoning baselines, VICO
surpasses them by $`+15.5\%`$ on average. Against the strongest
self-evolution baseline (MM-Zero), the three VICO variants surpass it by
$`+4.3\%`$ on the OOD benchmarks. Against the text-editing co-evolution
baseline (V-Zero), VICO outperforms it by $`+8.4\%`$ on the overlapping
benchmarks. Beyond open-source baselines, VICO-8B also outperforms
Gemini-2-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Pro by $`+5.2\%`$ and $`+2.5\%`$ on the
OOD benchmarks, showing that an 8B model trained through co-evolution
can compete with much larger proprietary VLMs.

VICO has strong generalization across OOD domains and models. As shown
in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"),
VICO-8B variants gain $`+5.2\%`$ on average across OOD benchmarks. The
transfer is strongest in mathematical reasoning: without math-specific
training, VICO-8B (CLEVR), VICO-8B (Chart), and VICO-8B (ZwZ) improve
over Qwen3-VL-8B by $`+5.5\%`$, $`+5.4\%`$, and $`+5.3\%`$ on MathVista,
MathVision, MathVerse, WeMath, and LogicVista. This suggests that VICO
learns transferable reasoning skills rather than domain-specific edit
shortcuts. By comparison, existing RLVR baselines transfer less
reliably: R1-OneVision-7B and MM-Eureka-Qwen-7B improve on one
benchmark, but Qwen2.5-based RLVR baselines drop by $`-7.3\%`$ on
average relative to their base models. VICO also transfers across
backbones.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
shows that VICO-Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Chart) and VICO-InternVL3-8B (Chart)
improve over their base models by $`+4.7\%`$ and $`+7.1\%`$ on average.

Table 5: Iterative co-evolution beats static augmentation. Strong
offline generators such as GPT-5 and Nano Banana improve ChartQA
accuracy, but they remain below actor-conditioned visual co-evolution,
which reaches $`89.1\%`$.

Editing images is more effective than rewriting text alone. We compare
visual-environment editing with text-only perturbation in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
Within the same VICO environment, image editing yields a $`+6.1\%`$ gain
in the evaluated reasoning benchmarks, while text-only perturbation
improves by only $`+2.4\%`$. The gap is especially clear on ChartQA,
where image editing gains $`+9.4\%`$ versus only $`+0.9\%`$ for
text-only perturbation. This finding is further supported by independent
evidence: in the separately developed V-Zero framework, text-only
perturbation also improves mathematical reasoning by only $`+1.8\%`$
over its base model. Together, these results show that the key
bottleneck is the editing modality itself: effective co-evolution
requires modifying the visual environment, not just rewriting the text.

![Refer to caption](2610.10782v1/figures/combined_four_panels.png)

Figure 3: VICO trains stably and induces an emergent curriculum. (a)
GRPO reward improves smoothly. (b) ChartQA accuracy peaks at Round 4
with a $`+12.2`$ gain. (c) Actor responses grow by $`+49\%`$, suggesting
harder tasks and longer reasoning. (d) Gains concentrate on
reasoning-heavy question types.

VICO trains stably and improves across training rounds.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")(a)
shows that the step-wise GRPO training score increases smoothly without
collapse or divergence. Across rounds,
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")(b)
shows that VICO steadily improves on ChartQA. Accuracy rises from
$`76.9\%`$ at the base model to $`89.1\%`$ at R4, giving a total gain of
$`+12.2\%`$. Each round contributes a positive gain. This improvement
also appears at the sample level. Appendix
Table [20](#A9.T20 "Table 20 ‣ I.3 Sample-Level Flip Analysis ‣ Appendix I Co-Evolution Dynamics and Qualitative Analysis ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
shows that R1 unlocks $`13.9\%`$ test samples, and the cumulative
unlocked fraction grows to $`16.1\%`$ by R4. These results show that
VICO accumulates new correct behaviors across rounds rather than
reflecting round-specific fluctuations.

VICO’s Gains concentrate on reasoning-heavy question types.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")(d)
breaks down ChartQA accuracy by task type. The largest gains appear in
multi-step reasoning, including ratio/percentage ($`+29.8\%`$), value
lookup ($`+20.1\%`$), and difference ($`+11.9\%`$). In contrast,
visually simpler tasks improve less, such as comparison ($`+7.1\%`$) and
counting ($`+8.2\%`$). The yes/no category slightly drops ($`-2.6\%`$),
likely because it is already saturated. These results suggest that VICO
mainly improves reasoning-intensive skills rather than simply boosting
easy visual recognition patterns.

VICO turns errors into correct answers with limited regression. To
understand where the gain of round 4 comes from, we compare each
sample’s correctness between the base model and our round 4 actor on the
ChartQA test set (Appendix
Table [19](#A9.T19 "Table 19 ‣ I.3 Sample-Level Flip Analysis ‣ Appendix I Co-Evolution Dynamics and Qualitative Analysis ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")).
VICO converts 365 samples from wrong to right ($`14.6\%`$), while only
64 samples flip from right to wrong ($`2.6\%`$). This gives an
improvement-to-regression ratio of $`\mathbf{5.7\times}`$. The net gain
of 301 samples corresponds to $`+12.0\%`$, closely matching the
aggregate accuracy gain of $`+12.2\%`$. Qualitatively, wrong-to-right
cases often show explicit step-by-step decomposition, whereas the base
model tends to give single-shot answers; examples are provided in
Appendix [I.5](#A9.SS5 "I.5 Chain-of-Thought Case Studies ‣ Appendix I Co-Evolution Dynamics and Qualitative Analysis ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
These results show that the gains mainly come from newly acquired
correct behaviors, not from trading off many previously correct samples.

### 5.3 Co-Evolution Dynamics, Capability Emergence, and Ablations

We then examine whether the actor–environment loop behaves as intended
and whether this loop is the source of the gains.

|                                     |                      |
|-------------------------------------|----------------------|
| Baselines                           | ChartQA ($`\Delta`$) |
| Base (Qwen3-VL-8B)                  | 76.9                 |
| Actor SFT only                      | 79.4 _(+2.5↑)        |
| Co-evolution (w/ Vanilla Re-writer) | 78.6 _(+1.7↑)        |
| Co-evolution (VICO)                 | 89.1 _(+12.2↑)       |

Table 6: Rewriter initialization is not enough; co-evolution unlocks the
full gain. Actor SFT (w/o co-training) and a vanilla EnvRewriter give
modest gains ($`+2.5\%`$ and $`+1.7\%`$), while an SFT-initialized
EnvRewriter optimized in the actor–environment loop reaches $`+12.2\%`$.

Both Rewriter SFT and the co-evolution loop are required.
Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.3 Co-Evolution Dynamics, Capability Emergence, and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
separates the roles of supervised initialization and iterative
co-evolution. Actor SFT alone improves ChartQA by only $`+2.5\%`$, so
stronger actor initialization cannot explain the full gain. Running the
co-evolution loop with a vanilla EnvRewriter gives only $`+1.7\%`$,
because the Rewriter cannot effectively produce executable edit plans.
Thus, the loop alone is also insufficient without a valid environment
policy. The full $`+12.2\%`$ gain appears only when the EnvRewriter is
SFT-initialized and then optimized through the iterative
actor–environment loop. This shows that Rewriter SFT provides valid
environment edits, while co-evolution turns those edits into
actor-aligned training signals.

The EnvRewriter learns bidirectional difficulty calibration. We compare
two domains with opposite initial actor competence: ChartQA starts easy
for the actor ($`\hat{p}_{\text{orig}}\approx 0.85`$), while ZwZ starts
hard ($`\hat{p}_{\text{orig}}\approx 0.21`$). The EnvRewriter adapts in
opposite directions. It makes ChartQA harder and lowers
$`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}`$, while making ZwZ easier and raising
$`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}`$. In both cases, $`\hat{p}_{\text{final}}`$
enters $`[0.35,0.65]`$ within the first few rounds
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Co-Evolution Dynamics, Capability Emergence, and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")).
This shows actor-relative calibration instead of random perturbation.

Stronger edits reflect learned decisions, not longer instructions. We
next ask whether the EnvRewriter becomes a stronger editor across
rounds. We measure edit intensity as
$`|\hat{p}_{\text{orig}}-\hat{p}_{\text{final}}|`$, the pass-rate shift
caused by an edit for the current actor. Edit intensity increases from
$`0.22`$ to $`0.51`$, showing that the EnvRewriter changes task
difficulty more effectively. This increase is not due to longer outputs:
the average instruction length remains nearly unchanged ($`973\to 981`$
tokens)
(Figure [10](#A5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ E.7 Pass-Rate Distribution Shift ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Analysis and Saturation ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
in the Appendix). In contrast, the actor’s response length grows by
$`+49\%`$ (Figure
[3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")(c)),
consistent with longer reasoning traces on harder tasks. These trends
provide behavioral evidence of co-adaptation: the EnvRewriter produces
more targeted edits, while the actor adapts with more elaborate
reasoning. Additional analyzes are provided in
Appendix [I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2 Editing Intensity and Response Length ‣ Appendix I Co-Evolution Dynamics and Qualitative Analysis ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
and
Appendix [I.5](#A9.SS5 "I.5 Chain-of-Thought Case Studies ‣ Appendix I Co-Evolution Dynamics and Qualitative Analysis ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

The iterative visual co-evolution loop drives the gains. We ablate
whether the improvement comes from the co-evolution loop, the stronger
offline data or RLVR-only training. First, we remove the loop and
compare it against static offline augmentation. As shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"),
stronger teachers improve the fixed corpus only modestly: Qwen3-VL-8B
self-generation, GPT-5, and Nano Banana reach $`78.64\%`$, $`80.10\%`$,
and $`81.91\%`$ on ChartQA. All remain below $`82\%`$. In contrast,
VICO-8B (Chart) reaches $`89.12\%`$, exceeding the strongest static
method by $`+7.21\%`$. Scaling the offline teacher from self-generation
to Nano Banana gives only $`+3.27\%`$, while adding the iterative loop
gives $`+7.21\%`$. Second, we keep the RLVR setup fixed but remove
Rewriter-driven environment adaptation. Across all VICO variants,
co-evolution outperforms Direct GRPO by $`+3.7\%`$ and Supervised GRPO
by $`+4.8\%`$ on average. These results show that the gains come from
VICO’s iterative, difficulty-aligned actor-environment co-evolution.

VICO is robust against imperfect image editing. Automatic image editors
may produce blank images, unchanged images, or image-label mismatches.
We therefore stress-test VICO by corrupting $`20\%`$ of the R1 training
data. As shown in
Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.3 Co-Evolution Dynamics, Capability Emergence, and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"),
the overall average performance drops by less than $`1\%`$. The noisy
model still remains well above the baseline model. This shows that VICO
does not require a flawless image editor: failed edits do not dominate
training, and the remaining valid samples are sufficient for stable
co-evolution. Additional details in
Appendix [H.4](#A8.SS4 "H.4 Robustness to Imperfect Image Editing ‣ Appendix H Ablation and Robustness Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

Image-generator capability does not replace co-evolution. Our editing
strategy must control difficulty while keeping labels verifiable. Simple
perturbations, such as noise, rotation, or blur, can lower the Actor’s
pass rate, but they mostly add perceptual noise and may shift samples
away from the task distribution. Strong image generators produce better
images, yet unconstrained generation can still cause answer drift or
ambiguous labels. In contrast, VICO edits verifiable visual structures
and preserves supervision through programmatic relabeling or
answer-preserving editing. Thus, strong generators are useful backends,
but not replacements for VICO: the core benefit is the actor-conditioned
loop that selects, verifies, and re-aligns edits using rollout feedback.
See
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Case Study: Co-Evolution Matters More Than Image-Generation Strength ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

## 6 Conclusion

We present VICO, a co-evolution framework that reframes visual reasoning
training as a dynamic, data-evolving co-evolution between an actor and
an EnvRewriter, rather than a model-evolving process over a static
corpus. By repurposing the rollout pass rate as a shared learning
signal, VICO jointly trains an actor and an EnvRewriter that edits
verifiable visual substructures toward the actor’s learning frontier,
producing difficulty-calibrated training samples without any additional
human annotation. Across nine multimodal benchmarks, VICO consistently
outperforms strong RLVR, self-evolution, and co-evolution baselines,
generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks unseen during training, and
remains stable across multiple VLM backbones, exceeding the strongest
self-evolution baseline by +4.3% on out-of-domain tasks while using up
to 160$`\times`$ fewer labeled samples. Together, these results suggest
that the bottleneck in visual reasoning post-training is *not the size
of the static corpus but the fixed nature of the environment itself*,
and that difficulty-aligned visual editing offers a scalable path
forward in domains where high-quality human annotation is costly to
obtain.

## Appendix A Limitations, Future Work, and Impact Statement

##### Limitations

Although VICO shows strong empirical gains across multimodal reasoning
benchmarks, several limitations remain. First, VICO relies on a
verifiable image-side structure for editing. In CLEVR and ChartQA, this
structure is provided by scene graphs or chart tables; in natural-image
VQA, it is approximated by protected region masks. Extending the
framework to visual domains without such structures or reliable region
annotations remains an important direction.

Second, VICO introduces additional compute costs because each round
estimates actor pass rates with multiple rollouts and updates both the
actor and the EnvRewriter. This cost is higher than that of one-shot
static augmentation, although it enables the training distribution to
adapt to the actor’s evolving capabilities.

Third, our evaluation focuses on visual reasoning tasks with verifiable
answers. Open-ended generation, dialog, and real-time interactive
environments are outside the current scope. Future work can study
adaptive difficulty targets, broader visual domains, and tighter
integration with more general-purpose image editors.

##### Future work

Future work can extend VICO to more complex multimodal tasks beyond
static image reasoning. We plan to broaden the framework to tasks that
require richer visual grounding, multi-image comparison, diagram
reasoning, and tool-assisted multimodal problem solving. These settings
require the environment to edit not only visual appearance but also
higher-level task structure while preserving verifiable supervision.

##### Impact Statement

VICO aims to reduce the reliance on large-scale human annotation for VLM
post-training by turning existing visual data into adaptive, label-valid
training samples. This may make visual reasoning training more scalable
and accessible, especially in domains where high-quality annotations are
expensive. At the same time, automatic image editing can introduce
artifacts, biases, or label drift if used without verification. Our
framework mitigates these risks through deterministic relabeling,
answer-preserving constraints, and filtering, but careful validation
remains necessary before applying similar systems to high-stakes
domains.

## Appendix B Implementation Details

### B.1 VICO: Algorithm Details

Require: Actor $`\pi_{a}`$, EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}`$, seed dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{seed}}=\{(x_{i},q_{i},a_{i},\sigma_{i})\}`$, number
of rounds $`T`$, rollouts per sample $`K`$, target pass rate $`\alpha`$,
difficulty filter threshold $`k_{\min}`$, RWR temperature $`\lambda`$

Ensure: Trained actor $`\pi_{a}`$, EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}`$

Initialize actor pool $`\mathcal{D}_{a}\leftarrow\varnothing`$,
EnvRewriter pool $`\mathcal{D}_{R}\leftarrow\varnothing`$

for round $`t=1,\dots,T`$ do

 Stage 1: Online Generation & Interaction

 Sample edit batch:
$`\mathcal{T}_{t}\leftarrow\{(x^{\prime}_{i},q^{\prime}_{i},a^{\prime}_{i})\}`$
where $`u_{i}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid x_{i},\sigma_{i})`$,
$`x^{\prime}_{i}=\mathcal{R}(u_{i}(\sigma_{i}))`$

 for each edited triple
$`(x^{\prime}_{i},q^{\prime}_{i},a^{\prime}_{i})\in\mathcal{T}_{t}`$ do

   Sample $`K`$ rollouts $`\{\hat{a}_{i,k}\}_{k=1}^{K}`$ from
$`\pi_{a}(\cdot\mid x^{\prime}_{i},q^{\prime}_{i})`$

   Compute actor reward
$`R_{\text{actor}}(\hat{a}_{i,k},a^{\prime}_{i})`$ for each rollout

   Compute pass rate $`\hat{p}_{i}\leftarrow k_{i}/K`$

   Compute EnvRewriter reward $`R_{\text{rewriter}}(\hat{p}_{i})`$

 end for

 Stage 2: Joint Update

 Update $`\pi_{a}`$ via GRPO on $`\mathcal{T}_{t}`$ to maximize
$`\mathbb{E}[R_{\text{actor}}]`$

 Filter:
$`\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}\leftarrow\{(x_{i},\sigma_{i},u_{i}):|\hat{p}_{i}-\alpha|\leq k_{\min}\}`$

 Build weighted SFT set:
$`\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{R}^{t}\leftarrow\{(x_{i},\sigma_{i},u_{i},w_{i}):w_{i}\propto\exp(\lambda R_{\text{rewriter}}(\hat{p}_i))\}`$

 Update $`\pi_{R}`$ via RWR on $`\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{R}^{t}`$ to
maximize $`\mathbb{E}[R_{\text{rewriter}}]`$

 Stage 3: Aggregation

 $`\mathcal{D}_{a}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{a}\cup\text{Valid}(\mathcal{T}_{t})`$

 $`\mathcal{D}_{R}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{R}\cup\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{R}^{t}`$

end for

Algorithm 1 VICO jointly updates the Actor and EnvRewriter from shared
rollouts. Each round generates edited tasks, evaluates Actor rollouts,
updates the Actor with task rewards, and updates the EnvRewriter with
difficulty-calibration rewards.

VICO trains an Actor and an EnvRewriter in an iterative
actor–environment loop. The Actor learns from verifiable rollout
rewards, while the EnvRewriter learns from the Actor’s empirical pass
rate on its edited samples. The two models share a common pool of
rollouts: each rollout simultaneously yields a task-level reward used to
update the Actor and a difficulty signal used to update the EnvRewriter,
enabling co-evolution without doubling the inference cost. The complete
training loop is summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ B.1 VICO: Algorithm Details ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
and described below.

##### Inputs and initialization

The pipeline starts from a seed visual dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{seed}}=\{(x,q,a,\sigma)\}`$, where $`x`$ is the
image, $`q`$ is the question, $`a`$ is the answer, and $`\sigma`$ is a
verifiable substructure when available, such as a CLEVR scene graph or a
ChartQA data table. We initialize the Actor $`\pi_{a}^{(0)}`$ and the
EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}^{(0)}`$ from the same pretrained VLM family. The
EnvRewriter is first SFT-initialized to produce executable edit
commands. Four hyperparameters control the loop: the number of rounds
$`T`$, the rollouts per sample $`K`$, the target pass rate $`\alpha`$
(we use $`\alpha=0.5`$), the difficulty filter threshold $`k_{\min}`$
that discards edits whose pass rate is too far from $`\alpha`$, and the
RWR temperature $`\lambda`$ that controls how sharply the EnvRewriter is
biased toward high-reward edits. Two online pools, the Actor pool
$`\mathcal{D}_{a}`$ and the EnvRewriter pool $`\mathcal{D}_{R}`$, are
initialized empty and grow throughout training.

##### Stage 1: Online generation and interaction

At the start of each round $`t`$, the EnvRewriter proposes a structured
edit command $`u_{i}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid x_{i},\sigma_{i})`$ over the
verifiable substructure $`\sigma_{i}`$ for every seed instance. A domain
renderer or editor produces the edited image
$`x^{\prime}_{i}=\mathcal{R}(u_{i}(\sigma_{i}))`$, and the answer
$`a^{\prime}_{i}`$ is either computed programmatically from the edited
structure or preserved by construction under the domain-specific
validity rules in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Data Sources and Verifiable Visual Editing ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
Thus, every retained sample is label-valid without model-based labeling.
For each edited triple
$`(x^{\prime}_{i},q^{\prime}_{i},a^{\prime}_{i})`$, the Actor samples
$`K`$ responses, and each response receives the rule-based Actor reward
defined in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Reward Functions and Difficulty Filtering ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
We then compute the empirical pass rate $`\hat{p}_{i}=k_{i}/K`$, where
$`k_{i}`$ is the number of correct rollouts, and map it to the
difficulty-calibration reward $`R_{\text{rewriter}}`$, which peaks when
$`\hat{p}_{i}`$ matches the target $`\alpha`$.

##### Stage 2: Joint update

The two models are updated from the same batch of rollouts, but with
different reward signals. Valid edited triples
$`(x^{\prime}_{t},q^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t})`$ are used to update
the Actor $`\pi_{a}`$ via GRPO to maximize
$`\mathbb{E}[R_{\text{actor}}]`$, leveraging the within-group advantage
normalization that makes GRPO robust to scale differences across edits.
The EnvRewriter $`\pi_{R}`$ is updated via Reward-Weighted Regression
(RWR): we first apply a difficulty filter, retaining only edits whose
pass rate falls within $`[\alpha-k_{\min},\alpha+k_{\min}]`$, and then
construct a weighted SFT set in which each retained edit transition is
weighted by $`\exp(\lambda R_{\text{rewriter}})`$. Fine-tuning
$`\pi_{R}`$ on this set biases it toward edits that land close to the
target band. We additionally apply a KL penalty to the initial
EnvRewriter and cap the per-step KL to prevent the editor from drifting
into degenerate or off-distribution edit distributions.

##### Stage 3: Aggregation

After each round, valid edited triples (those that render successfully
and pass label-consistency checks) are appended to the Actor pool
$`\mathcal{D}_{a}`$, while the weighted edit transitions are appended to
the EnvRewriter pool $`\mathcal{D}_{R}`$. Both pools persist across
rounds, so the Actor sees an increasingly diverse set of edited tasks,
and the EnvRewriter learns from an increasingly informative history of
difficulty signals. The updated Actor and EnvRewriter then become the
starting point for the next round.

##### Why this differs from static RLVR?

The key distinction from static RLVR is that the empirical pass rate
$`\hat{p}`$ is not used only as a filtering statistic. It is also reused
as an actor-relative supervision signal for the EnvRewriter, allowing
the visual environment to track the Actor’s current capability.
Crucially, the loop requires no new human-labeled QA: the seed
representation $`\sigma_{i}`$ provides the editable interface, and
labels for edited samples are either recomputed or preserved through
explicit validity constraints.

### B.2 Actor GRPO Training Details

For the Actor $`\pi_{a}`$, we use GRPO with rule-based rewards. For each
edited prompt, we sample multiple on-policy rollouts and score them with
exact-match answer verification plus a format check. Unless otherwise
stated, rollout sampling uses temperature $`0.7`$, top-$`p=1.0`$, and a
maximum response length of $`3{,}824`$ tokens, matching the zero-shot
evaluation setting in the main text.

In the ChartQA multi-round runs, each round trains on approximately
$`1500`$–$`2500`$ EnvRewriter-generated modified training images,
together with a fixed regularization set of $`2{,}000`$ original ChartQA
samples. The resulting Actor checkpoint initializes the next round.

### B.3 EnvRewriter SFT and RWR Details

The EnvRewriter is trained in two stages. First, we initialize it with
format-aware SFT on verified edit demonstrations generated by GPT-5.
This stage teaches the model to produce structured, executable edit
commands, use the available edit operations, and propose edits that
adjust task difficulty while preserving label verifiability. Second,
during co-evolution, we update the learned EnvRewriter using
reward-weighted regression over valid edit transitions collected through
interaction with the Actor.

For each executed edit, the current Actor produces $`K`$ rollouts on the
resulting sample. The empirical pass rate $`\hat{p}`$ is used to compute
the edit’s RWR weight according to the bell-shaped difficulty objective
in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Reward Functions and Difficulty Filtering ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
These weights are computed from the outcome of each edit turn. Invalid
or unexecutable edits, as well as edits outside the RWR difficulty band,
are excluded from the RWR target set. This encourages the EnvRewriter to
concentrate its probability mass on valid edits near the Actor’s
learnable zone. Actor training data are constructed separately: samples
that satisfy execution and label-validity requirements may be retained
even when their pass rates fall outside the RWR difficulty band.

##### GPT-5 as a strategic trajectory generator.

We use GPT-5 to generate editing demonstrations for training the
EnvRewriter. Given a seed sample, its editable structure, the current
Actor’s empirical pass rate, the target difficulty band, and the
domain-specific edit schema, GPT-5 proposes a structured edit command
intended to adjust the task’s difficulty. The command is executed by the
environment, and the resulting sample is evaluated by the Actor. The
execution outcome and Actor feedback can then be included in the context
for subsequent edits, producing actor-conditioned editing trajectories.
GPT-5 provides the edit proposals, but it does not serve as the
authority for either ground-truth labels or training rewards. Labels are
obtained through domain-specific recomputation or checked for answer
preservation, depending on the edit setting, while difficulty is
measured using Actor rollouts. We construct the SFT dataset from
executable, verified demonstrations whose edits move the Actor’s pass
rate closer to the target pass rate. These demonstrations supervise both
the edit-command format and the choice of editing strategies.

##### EnvRewriter interface.

The EnvRewriter is an LVLM policy initialized from the same model family
as the Actor and SFT-initialized to produce executable edit commands.
Its input contains the image, question, answer, editable structure
$`\sigma`$, current Actor pass rate $`\hat{p}`$, target pass rate
$`\alpha`$, and the domain-specific tool schema. Its output is a
structured tool call with fields tool, params, and reasoning. For
example, in ChartQA, the EnvRewriter may output a chart_rerender command
that edits the underlying CSV table and re-renders the chart. The
command is executed by the domain renderer or image editor, and the
resulting sample is kept only if it passes the validity checks in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Seed Visual Data and Verifiable Sample Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
Full prompts and tool schemas are provided in
Appendix [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 EnvRewriter Prompt ‣ Appendix F Evaluation Protocols and Prompt Templates ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").

### B.4 Reward Functions and Difficulty Filtering

##### Actor Reward.

The Actor reward is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{\text{actor}}(q^{\prime},o)=\begin{cases}+1,&\text{if }\mathrm{FormatCorrect}(o)\wedge\mathrm{AnswerCorrect}(o),\\
-1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (B.1) |

##### EnvRewriter Reward.

For each executed edit, the empirical pass rate on the resulting sample
is $`\hat{p}=k/K`$, where $`k`$ is the number of correct Actor rollouts
under $`R_{\text{actor}}`$. The EnvRewriter reward is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{\text{rewriter}}(\hat{p})=\exp\left(-\beta(\hat{p}-\alpha)^{2}\right),
``` |  | (B.2) |

where $`\beta>0`$ controls sharpness. We use $`\alpha=0.5`$,
$`\beta=4.0`$, and $`k_{\min}=0.15`$ for the difficulty filter.

##### Difficulty filter.

The reward encourages edits whose resulting samples have pass rates near
the Actor’s learning frontier. In practice, we keep a sweet-zone band
around $`\alpha=0.5`$ and discard invalid or poorly calibrated edits
from EnvRewriter updates. This prevents the EnvRewriter from overfitting
to samples that are already solved or impossible for the current Actor.

## Appendix C Data Sources and Verifiable Visual Editing

This appendix describes how VICO produces label-valid training samples
across three visual domains. The key point is that different domains
provide different forms of verifiability.

For CLEVR, VICO edits an explicit scene graph and recomputes the answer
programmatically by executing the original question program. For
ChartQA, VICO edits the underlying CSV table and uses a two-tier
verification rule: Tier 1 recovers the new answer by entity-anchored
lookup in the edited table, while Tier 2 keeps CSV values fixed and
preserves the original answer by construction. For natural-image VQA,
where no complete symbolic state is available, VICO uses
answer-preserving regional editing: the question and answer remain
fixed, while the EnvRewriter edits only non-target visual regions.

Thus, VICO uses two label-validity mechanisms: deterministic
recomputation when the answer can be derived from the edited structure,
and constrained answer preservation when the answer-bearing structure
must remain fixed.

### C.1 Seed Data Sources

VICO uses a small seed set to initialize each visual reasoning domain.
For compositional reasoning, we sample CLEVR images with their scene
graphs and question programs. For chart reasoning, we sample ChartQA
training images together with their underlying data tables. For
natural-image VQA, we sample ZwZ images, which provide answer-relevant
region annotations. We use these regions to identify target objects and
preserve the original question-answer pair during editing.

### C.2 Overview of the Three Editing Arms

Table [11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ C.2 Overview of the Three Editing Arms ‣ Appendix C Data Sources and Verifiable Visual Editing ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
summarizes the three editing arms. CLEVR supports full deterministic
answer recomputation from the edited scene graph. ChartQA uses a
two-tier table rule: Tier 1 updates the answer by entity-anchored lookup
in the edited CSV table, while Tier 2 preserves the answer under
constrained table edits. The natural-image VQA arm follows a different
rule: it keeps the original question and answer unchanged and only edits
regions outside the answer-relevant target objects.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Arm |  Editing interface |  Answer rule |
|  CLEVR |  Scene graph edits over objects, attributes, and relations; rendered with Blender. |  Recompute $`a^{\prime}`$ by re-executing the question program. |
|  ChartQA |  CSV/table edits rendered with matplotlib. |  Tier 1: entity-anchored lookup; Tier 2: keep $`a^{\prime}=a`$ under constrained edits. |
|  ZwZ |  SAM3 masks with protected target objects; edit only non-target regions. |  Keep $`q^{\prime}=q`$ and $`a^{\prime}=a`$ under target-object protection. |

Table 11: VICO uses three editing arms for verifiable visual variation.
CLEVR recomputes answers from scene graphs, ChartQA uses a two-tier
table rule, and ZwZ preserves answers by protecting target objects.

### C.3 CLEVR: Scene-Graph Editing

For CLEVR, the editable structure $`\sigma`$ is the scene graph paired
with each image. Each scene graph specifies a set of objects, with each
object carrying attributes such as shape, color, material, and size, as
well as pairwise spatial relations such as left-of, right-of, front, and
behind. Questions are generated from question-program templates over the
scene graph, so the same program can be re-executed on the edited graph
to produce $`a^{\prime}`$.

##### Edit operations.

The EnvRewriter outputs an edit command $`u`$ in one of four categories:
(i) attribute change, which modifies the color, material, or size of a
target object; (ii) category swap, which changes an object’s shape among
cube, sphere, and cylinder; (iii) entity add/remove, which inserts or
deletes objects while preserving renderability; and (iv) relation
modification, which repositions objects to alter spatial relations. Each
operation acts on the scene graph rather than on pixels, so
$`u(\sigma)`$ remains a fully specified renderable scene.

##### Renderer.

We use Blender with the original CLEVR rendering script to produce
$`x^{\prime}=\mathcal{R}(u(\sigma))`$. Camera parameters, lighting, and
material shaders are kept consistent with the original rendering
pipeline to avoid stylistic drift.

##### Answer derivation.

We retain the original question program and re-execute it on
$`u(\sigma)`$ to obtain $`a^{\prime}`$. For example, if the original
program is count(filter(color=red, shape=cube)) and the edit changes one
red cube into a blue cube, the new answer decreases by one. Because
program execution on a discrete scene graph is exact, CLEVR samples are
label-valid by construction.

##### Failure mode.

An edit is discarded if it makes the question ambiguous or
non-executable. For example, if an edit creates multiple possible
referents for a question that assumes a unique object, the sample is
removed before training.

### C.4 ChartQA: Table-Level Editing and Re-rendering

For chart reasoning, the editable structure $`\sigma`$ is the CSV table
underlying each chart. The EnvRewriter edits the table-level
representation rather than chart pixels, and matplotlib re-renders the
edited table into a new chart image. This allows VICO to adjust visual
and numerical difficulty while keeping label validity controlled by the
table.

##### Tier construction.

For each ChartQA seed sample, we first apply an automatic label-to-cell
matching heuristic. We scan the CSV table and match value cells against
the original answer. If exactly one cell matches, the sample is assigned
to Tier 1. Let $`(r^{\star},j^{\star})`$ denote the matched answer cell,
and let $`e^{\star}`$ denote the row entity at $`r^{\star}`$ in the
original table. If no cell matches, or multiple cells match, the sample
is assigned to Tier 2. Tier 2 often includes derived-answer cases such
as ratios, percentages, or differences, or ambiguous duplicate values.

##### Edit operations.

For Tier 1, the EnvRewriter may modify table values, add near-match
distractor rows, increase chart density, or sharpen contrasts. After
editing, the answer is recovered by entity-anchored lookup in the edited
table:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a^{\prime}=\mathrm{table}^{\prime}[\mathrm{entity}=e^{\star},j^{\star}].
``` |  |

This lookup avoids relying on the original row index after row insertion
or reordering. For Tier 2, the EnvRewriter keeps CSV values fixed and
only varies rendering style or other answer-preserving visual factors.
The label is therefore kept as $`a^{\prime}=a`$ by construction.

##### Renderer.

We re-render charts with matplotlib using the same chart type and style
configuration as the source chart whenever possible, including chart
type, color palette, axis labels, fonts, and gridlines.

##### Failure mode.

We discard edits that violate the table schema, remove or duplicate the
Tier 1 anchor entity $`e^{\star}`$, remove the target column
$`j^{\star}`$, produce no numeric columns, fail rendering, or break the
Tier 2 invariance constraint by changing CSV values. Numerical edits are
bounded to keep the rendered chart visually plausible.

### C.5 ZwZ: Answer-Preserving Natural-Image Editing

For natural-image VQA, VICO does not attempt to recompute a new answer
from a full symbolic scene representation. Instead, it preserves the
original question-answer pair. Given a seed sample $`(x,q,a)`$, the
edited sample is $`(x^{\prime},q,a)`$, where $`q^{\prime}=q`$ and
$`a^{\prime}=a`$.

The key assumption is that the answer is grounded in a set of
answer-relevant target objects. ZwZ provides answer-relevant region
annotations, and we use SAM3 to decompose the image into object-level
masks. Masks that overlap the answer-relevant region are treated as
target objects. These target objects form the protected region
$`\sigma^{+}`$. All other object masks and background regions form the
editable complement $`\sigma^{-}`$.

##### Edit operations.

The EnvRewriter receives the image, question, answer, object masks,
protected target objects, and current Actor pass-rate signal. It then
proposes edits restricted to $`\sigma^{-}`$. Typical edits include
adding distractor objects outside the target region, modifying
background clutter, changing the appearance of non-target objects, or
introducing visually plausible distractors that do not alter the
answer-relevant target objects. The EnvRewriter is not allowed to edit,
occlude, remove, or semantically change the protected target objects.

##### Rendering.

The original image, the protected target-object mask, and the edit
command are passed to an external image editor. The editor modifies only
the editable complement and returns the edited image $`x^{\prime}`$.
Unlike CLEVR or ChartQA, this step is not treated as deterministic
symbolic rendering. It is an answer-preserving image-editing step under
a protected-region constraint.

##### Answer rule.

For ZwZ, the answer is not recomputed. We keep the original question and
answer:

|     |                                   |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       q^{\prime}=q,\qquad a^{\prime}=a.
       ```                                |     |

The Actor reward therefore compares the model’s prediction against the
original answer $`a`$. This distinguishes natural-image VQA from the
structured arms, where $`a^{\prime}`$ is programmatically recomputed.

##### Failure mode.

An edit is discarded if it touches the protected target objects, changes
the visual evidence needed to answer the question, or introduces new
content that would make the original answer ambiguous. For example, if
the question depends on counting target objects, adding another object
of the same relevant category is rejected. If the question depends on a
spatial relation involving a target object, edits that change that
relation are rejected. This conservative filtering keeps the
natural-image VQA arm answer-preserving rather than relabeled.

### C.6 Filtering Invalid or Ambiguous Edits

Across all editing arms, we discard edits that fail label-validity or
execution checks.

First, the edited sample must be executable by the corresponding
renderer or image editor. For CLEVR, the scene graph must render
successfully in Blender. For ChartQA, the edited CSV must satisfy the
table schema and render successfully with matplotlib. For ZwZ, the image
editor must preserve the protected target-object region.

Second, the edited sample must preserve a valid answer. For CLEVR, the
question program must be executable on the edited scene graph to compute
$`a^{\prime}`$. For ChartQA Tier 1, the anchor entity $`e^{\star}`$ and
target column $`j^{\star}`$ must remain valid and addressable in the
edited table so that
$`a^{\prime}=\mathrm{table}^{\prime}[\mathrm{entity}=e^{\star},j^{\star}]`$
can be recovered by lookup. For ChartQA Tier 2, the edit must satisfy
the invariance constraint: CSV values remain fixed and the original
answer is kept as $`a^{\prime}=a`$. For ZwZ, the original answer remains
valid because protected target regions are not edited.

Third, the edited sample must provide useful difficulty for the current
Actor. We measure this by the empirical pass rate $`\hat{p}`$ after
Actor rollouts. Invalid, ambiguous, unexecutable, or out-of-band edits
are removed from the EnvRewriter update set.

### C.7 Dataset and Edited Sample Visualizations

Figures [5](#A4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ D.1 CLEVR Scene-Graph Editing Examples ‣ Appendix D Image Editing Case Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"),
[6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ D.2 ChartQA Table-Level Editing Examples ‣ Appendix D Image Editing Case Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning"),
and
[7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ D.3 ZwZ Answer-Preserving Regional Editing Examples ‣ Appendix D Image Editing Case Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
show representative visual examples for the three editing arms. For
CLEVR, edits are applied to a scene graph and the answer $`a^{\prime}`$
is recomputed by executing the original question program. For ChartQA,
Tier 1 examples recover $`a^{\prime}`$ by entity-anchored lookup in the
edited CSV table, while Tier 2 examples preserve $`a^{\prime}=a`$
through constrained table edits. For ZwZ, the original question and
answer are retained, while answer-relevant target objects are protected
and only non-target regions are edited. Together, these examples show
the two label-validity mechanisms used by VICO: deterministic
recomputation when an answer can be derived from the edited structure,
and constrained answer preservation when the answer-bearing structure
must remain fixed.

### C.8 Robustness to Tool Failures and Difficulty Alignment as the Bottleneck

Renderer or editor failures may produce non-renderable scenes, invalid
charts, or protected-region violations. In VICO, these failures are
filtered before EnvRewriter updates: invalid, label-breaking, or
out-of-band edits contribute no gradient to $`\pi_{R}`$. This biases the
EnvRewriter toward edit plans that are executable, label-valid, and
useful for the current Actor.
Appendix [H.4](#A8.SS4 "H.4 Robustness to Imperfect Image Editing ‣ Appendix H Ablation and Robustness Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning")
further stress-tests this assumption by corrupting 20% of R1 training
data and shows that performance drops by less than one point.

### D.2 ChartQA Table-Level Editing Examples

We present the ChartQA edits shown in
Figure [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ D.2 ChartQA Table-Level Editing Examples ‣ Appendix D Image Editing Case Studies ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
Each seed sample is associated with an underlying data table table, a
question $`q`$, and an original answer $`a`$. Conditioned on the current
Actor pass rate $`\hat{p}`$, the EnvRewriter generates a table-level
edit aimed at the desired difficulty. To make the sample harder, it may
add near-match rows, distractor series, or more confusable values; to
make it easier, it may remove distractors or sharpen relevant contrasts.
The edit is applied to table to produce $`\text{table}^{\prime}`$, which
is then re-rendered into a new chart.

We use the same two-tier verification rule as in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Seed Visual Data and Verifiable Sample Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning").
For Tier 1 samples, the answer maps to a unique CSV cell
$`(r^{\star},j^{\star})`$. Let $`e^{\star}`$ denote the row entity at
$`r^{\star}`$ in the original table. After editing, the new answer is
recovered by entity-anchored lookup:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a^{\prime}=\mathrm{table}^{\prime}[\mathrm{entity}=e^{\star},j^{\star}].
``` |  |

This avoids relying on the original row index after rows are inserted or
reordered.

For Tier 2 samples, the answer has no unique cell mapping, such as no
match or multiple matches. These cases often include derived quantities
such as ratios, differences, or percentages. For Tier 2, the EnvRewriter
keeps CSV values fixed and only varies rendering style or other
answer-preserving visual factors, so the label remains $`a^{\prime}=a`$
by construction. In both tiers, no human relabeling or LLM judgment is
used.
